changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from CV Austere & Disaster Medicine Part Two: white-phosphorus pathophysiology, comparative incendiary-agent table, prehospital management sequence, and the critical errors to avoid.

summary: White phosphorus is an incendiary munition, not a classic chemical agent, and its injuries are categorically unlike thermal burns — embedded particles keep burning in tissue, phosphoric acid drives hypocalcemia within the hour, and systemic absorption is fatal under 10% BSA. The management is deny oxygen, remove particles, keep the wound wet, and monitor calcium.
whyThisMatters: Incendiary agents are encountered in current conflicts regardless of legal status, and the field intervention decides the outcome — recognition of white phosphorus, and not treating it like a thermal or napalm burn, is the single most critical step. The mistakes are lethal and specific: extinguishing WP the way you would smother napalm, letting the wound dry in transport, debriding in bright light, or assuming a small burn is safe when systemic absorption can kill under 10% BSA.
clinicalTakeaway: Suspect white phosphorus from a garlic odor, bright yellow-white flame, white smoke, and particles that glow green in a darkened room. Remove all clothing, pick out visible particles with forceps (never bare hands) into water, and irrigate or immerse continuously — you are denying oxygen, not extinguishing a fire. Cover with saline-soaked or hydrogel dressings and keep them wet through transport. Get an ECG and ionized calcium early: hypocalcemia and QT prolongation can appear within one hour; give IV calcium for symptomatic hypocalcemia. Never use copper sulfate, and never apply the napalm smother protocol to WP.

items: Physical: solid, chalk-like, waxy. Ignites spontaneously in air at 34 °C, burns at ~800 °C locally with a bright yellow-white flame. Highly lipid-soluble — penetrates deeply through subcutaneous fat.

Smell: garlic-like odor, easily confused with sulfur mustard. Distinguish by combustion — WP ignites immediately with visible flame and particles glow green in darkness; sulfur mustard has delayed onset and no immediate combustion.
Self-sustaining combustion: embedded particles keep burning as long as oxygen is available. Do NOT extinguish — deny oxygen instead. Particles phosphoresce green — dim the room to locate them.

Dual mechanism: thermal injury from direct burning plus chemical injury from phosphoric acid formed during combustion. Deep full-thickness necrotic wounds that heal far more slowly than pure thermal burns.

Systemic toxicity: phosphoric acid consumes calcium during neutralization → hypocalcemia within hours, hyperphosphatemia, QT prolongation, arrhythmias, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity. Fatal at less than 10% BSA from systemic absorption.

items: 1. Scene safety — identify by garlic odor, bright yellow flame, white smoke, glowing particles. Avoid WP smoke (phosphorus pentoxide forms a phosphoric-acid aerosol → chemical pneumonitis). Remove all clothing immediately — burning particles on fabric reignite.

2. Particle removal — use forceps or tools, never bare hands. Dim the environment so particles glow green; remove all visible particles into a water container. Do not let particles dry — they reignite.

3. Continuous irrigation — immerse or continuously irrigate with cold water or saline. High-pressure syringe irrigation dislodges embedded particles. Water denies oxygen and cools thermal damage. Do not stop until all particles are out and the wound is covered.
4. Moist dressing — saline-soaked gauze or hydrogel; keep moist throughout transport. Covered, moist wounds will not reignite. Mineral oil is an acceptable alternative where water is limited.

5. Systemic monitoring — ECG for QT prolongation from hypocalcemia (can develop within one hour). Labs: ionized calcium, phosphate, LFTs, BMP, CBC, coags. IV calcium gluconate for symptomatic hypocalcemia. ICU-level monitoring for significant exposure.

body.text: Critical errors to avoid: do NOT use copper sulfate (historically used to identify WP particles; abandoned — causes fatal hemolysis and hepatotoxicity). Do NOT let the wound dry in transport — dry WP reignites on air contact. Do NOT debride in bright light — the phosphorescent glow is what confirms particle location. Do NOT assume a small burn area is safe — systemic absorption can be fatal under 10% BSA. Do NOT use the napalm protocol (smothering) for WP — these are opposite approaches.
